claims.text: The proposed target material is a PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy nanoparticle.
A mixture of Pt, Pd, Co, Cu, and Ni salts constitutes a single-source precursor.
Inhibiting precursor mobility during low-temperature single-source synthesis favors formation of a mixed, single-phase HEA nanoparticle.
Rapid quenching during reduction arrests atomic diffusion more strongly than gradual cooling.
Rapid quenching yields a more homogeneous, single-phase PtPdCoCuNi alloy than gradual cooling.
Rapid quenching freezes stochastic mixing of the metal atoms.
Gradual cooling permits atomic rearrangement that can produce compositional inhomogeneity and local phase segregation.
Rapidly quenched PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles contain a higher proportion of isolated Pt and Pd active sites than gradually cooled nanoparticles.
Isolated Pt and Pd sites enhance nitrobenzene adsorption and catalytic turnover.
Segregated or non-uniform phases diminish catalytic activity relative to homogeneous atomic mixing.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will have a higher turnover frequency or selectivity for nitrobenzene hydrogenation than gradually cooled nanoparticles.
DRIFTS and XPS signal shifts can evidence the proposed isolated Pt and Pd sites.
The balance of linear and bridging CO adsorption features in DRIFTS measures noble-metal site isolation in this alloy.
TEM and XPS can establish the spatial and compositional homogeneity needed for the comparison.
The proposed mechanism is bounded to single-source-precursor reduction below 100 °C in an inert atmosphere.
Cooling-rate effects may be negligible when atomic mobility is already strongly limited at the reduction temperature.

contradictions.description: The material is alternately described as a 'single-source precursor' and as a mixture of separate metal salts. Those are not necessarily the same precursor architecture, leaving the proposed starting state internally ambiguous.
